summary: Defines an extension to the Extensible Provisioning Protocol for carrying information about how a telephone number behind an ENUM domain was validated. It extends the domain name mapping so registries can record validation details. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a phone number gets an internet address, someone checks it is really yours. This adds a place to write down how that check was done.

questions: how to record enum validation information
how to update enum validation info in epp
subtitle: An EPP extension that lets a registry store how a phone number behind an ENUM domain name was validated.

tldr.problem: Only the assignee of an E.164 number should be able to register its ENUM domain name, so registries need a way to record the validation that was done.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends the EPP domain name mapping with an XML framework of add, rem, chg and inf elements that carry validation information, whose content is extensible.
tldr.outcome: Registries can add, change, remove and retrieve validation information with domain commands. The details of validation methods are left to local policy.

today: RFC 5076 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 5076 describes a framework for mapping ENUM validation information onto version 1.0 of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP). It extends the EPP domain name mapping (RFC 3731) and is specified in XML and XML Schema. Understanding the EPP core protocol (RFC 3730) is necessary to follow it.

ENUM (RFC 3761) uses the DNS to identify services tied to an E.164 telephone number. As RFC 4725 describes, usually only the assignee of the number has the right to register the matching ENUM domain name. A validation process therefore has to run before the name goes into the DNS, to make sure the domain holder is the assignee.

The RFC does not define validation methods, and does not fix the content of the validation information, because local legislation and procedures vary. It does include a working example, which has been an integral part of the Swiss ENUM trial.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone number should only get an internet address if it is yours. The registry needs a note of how that was checked, and this defines the note-taking format, not the checking itself.

sections.title: Design Requirements
sections.content:
Four requirements drive the design:

  • The design shall allow multiple policies and validation procedures.
  • It shall be possible to transmit validation information with EPP domain object requests and responses.
  • It shall be possible to add, modify and remove validation information.
  • It shall be possible to retrieve validation information stored in the ENUM Registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The note format has to fit many different rules, travel with normal requests, be editable, and be readable later.

sections.title: Object Attributes
sections.content:
The extension adds elements to the EPP domain name mapping. An ENUM domain name is an E.164 number translated into domain name syntax. Four commands handle validation information at the registry: add, rem (revoke), chg (change) and inf (get information).

Each validation is identified by an id attribute, a character string. It MUST be unique at least within the same ENUM domain name, and it is RECOMMENDED to be unique per ENUM registry so it stays unique after a transfer. It is usually assigned by the ENUM registrar and is required to revoke or change stored information.

The <validationInfo> element can hold any adequately documented element, because it uses the XML Schema <any> element. How many <validationInfo> elements a domain may have is subject to local policy.

The RFC also gives an optional example content, <simpleVal>. A fully compliant implementation does not need to implement it. Its elements are methodID (up to 63 characters), validationEntityID and registrarID (each 3 to 16 characters, both optional), executionDate, and an optional expirationDate, the last two being XML Schema dates.
sections.plainLanguage: Each check gets a tag number. The note itself can hold whatever the local rules need, and the example note says who checked, which method they used, when, and until when.

sections.title: How the EPP Commands Change
sections.content:
Whether the extension is used in a request or response depends on local policy. For example, a registry might require it for create, update and info but not for transfer and renew.

No elements are added to the check command or response, the info command, the transfer response, or the delete command and response. The info response gains an <e164val:infData> element in the EPP <extension>, holding one or more <e164val:inf> elements, each with an id.

The create, renew and transfer commands MUST carry an <extension> containing <e164val:create>, <e164val:renew> or <e164val:transfer>, which holds one or more <e164val:add> elements with an id and a <validationInfo> child. The update command carries <e164val:update> with any mix of add, rem and chg elements; rem has no children. Responses to these commands are as in the domain mapping.
sections.plainLanguage: Normal requests get an extra attachment with the check notes. Asking for info returns the notes, and update can add, drop or fix individual notes by tag.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content: The formal syntax is a complete XML Schema, suitable for automated validation of EPP XML instances, for the framework namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:e164val-1.0. A second schema defines the optional example under urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:e164valex-1.1. The create, renew and transfer elements share one type, and update has its own.
sections.plainLanguage: A strict rulebook in machine-readable form lets computers check that a note is written correctly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension adds no security services beyond those of EPP, the EPP domain name mapping and the protocol layers EPP uses. ENUM's own security considerations apply as well.

Validation information often contains sensitive personal information, so it is RECOMMENDED that it be returned in an info response only to the sponsoring client.
sections.plainLanguage: The check notes can hold private details, so only the registrar in charge of the domain should be allowed to read them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: Four URIs were registered under the IETF XML registry mechanism: the namespaces urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:e164val-1.0 and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:e164valex-1.1, and the schemas urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:e164val-1.0 and urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:e164valex-1.1.
sections.plainLanguage: The names used in the format were put on an official list so nobody else reuses them.
